title.narrative: Second South West Indian Ocean Fisheries Governance and Shared Growth Project - Madagascar

description.narrative: The Project Development Objective is to improve the management of selected fisheries at regional, national and community levels andto increase access by targeted fishers to alternative livelihood activities.

The development objective of the Second South West Indian Ocean Fisheries Governance and Shared Growth Project for Southern Africa is to improve the management of selected fisheries at regional, national and community levels and to increase access by targeted fishers to alternative livelihood activities. The project has comprises four components. 1) The first component, enhanced regional collaboration promotes the implementation of Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC) Resolutions in the South West Indian Ocean (SWIO) countries enhancing their compliance with their international fisheries obligations. It provides a coordination mechanism between African and Indian Ocean Developing Island States (AIODIS) for collaborating and sharing their own experiences to address some of their specific challenges and strengthens the newly created Indian Ocean Federation of Artisanal Fishers (FEdEration des Pêcheurs Artisans de l’OcEan Indien, FPAOI); 2) The Second component, strengthening capacities for priority fisheries management primarily targets policies, strategies, institutions, legal frameworks, and actions by the public sector necessary to improve priority fisheries management and performance and sustain regional marine environmental health and resilience to climate change. It will be backed by applied research activities aimed at understanding the resource base and building human and institutional capacity necessary to implement fisheries policies and management plans. 3) The third component, strengthening capacities for engagement in alternative fishing practices and livelihoods activities supports the fisheries management activities building acceptance and adherence to the fisheries management plans by the targeted communities. This component directly benefits the targeted local population by providing financial transfers, training, and small community infrastructure. 4) The fourth component, project management and coordination will support regional project coordination, implementation and management, country level implementation and management, and monitoring and evaluation (M&E) at regional and country levels.

condition.narrative: 10. The Recipient shall prepare, under terms of reference satisfactory to the Association, and furnish to the Association not laterthan January 15 in each calendar year, for the Association's consideration, a proposed work plan of activities to be included underthe Project for the following calendar year, such plan to include an implementation schedule and budget and financing plantherefor. (Schedule 2, Section I.H)

11. The recipient should ensure that no surveillance activities (or other Project activities relating to enforcement that requirephysical access) will be carried out under the Project in the maritime geographical areas of, or around, what is described asBassas da India, Europa Island, the Glorioso Islands and Juan de Nova Island, and Banc du Geyser.(Schedule 2, Section I.E,paragraph 6)

2. The Recipient shall review with the Association, on or about September 30, 2020, or such later date as the Association shallrequest, a report on the progress of the Project and shall take all measures required to ensure the efficient completion of theProject and the achievement of the objectives thereof, based on the conclusions and recommendations of the said report and theAssociation's views on the matter. (Schedule 2, Section II.B)

2. The Commission shall prepare, under terms of reference satisfactory to the Association, and furnish to the Association not laterthan January 15 in each calendar year, for the Association's consideration, a proposed work plan of activities to be included underthe Project for the following calendar year, such plan to include an implementation schedule and budget and financing plantherefor. (Schedule 2, Section I.E)

2. The Recipient shall ensure that no works are commenced under the Project, until and unless: (i) the Recipient shall haveverified, through its own staff, outside experts, or existing environmental/social institutions, that the works meet theenvironmental and/or social management requirements, if applicable, of appropriate national and local authorities and that theycomply with the review procedures set forth in the Environmental and Social Management Framework (ESMF) and/or Process Framework(PF), as the case may be, and the provisions of the National Project Implementation Manual; and (ii) if required, the Recipientshall have prepared and adopted the Social Impact Assessment (ESIA), the Environmental and Social Management Plan (ESMP) and/orPlan of Action (PA), as the case may be, and the same documents have been consulted upon and disclosed as approved by theAssociation. (Schedule 2, Section I.D.I.1)

3. The Recipient shall ensure that the Project is implemented in accordance with the provisions of the ESMF and/or PF, as the casemay, and each of the ESMP, ESIA, and/or the Plan of Action, as the case may be, in a manner satisfactory to the Association, andthat none of the provisions of the aforementioned documents is amended or waived without the prior written agreement of theAssociation. (Schedule 2, Section I.D.I.2)

4. The Recipient shall take all action necessary on its behalf to carry out the PA with due diligence and efficiency and at alltimes provide the funds necessary therefor and to ensure that, during Project implementation, no restriction to access to fishinggrounds under the Project is enforced until and unless the Association shall have approved the site-specific PA. (Schedule 2,Section I.D.II)

5. All surveillance activities carried out by the Recipient shall be under the control of the Centre de Surveillance des Pêches andshall be carried out by, or under the control of, civilian authorities, under terms of reference limited to fisheries surveillance.(Schedule 2, Section I.E, paragraph 1)

6. The Recipient shall ensure that all works, goods, services, and Operating Costs financed out of the proceeds of the Credit areused exclusively by, or under the control of, civilian authorities for the purposes of the Project, and not for any militarypurpose, or for any criminal investigation, prosecution or proceedings, or for any other purposes unrelated to the objectives ofthe Project. (Schedule 2, Section I.E, paragraph 2)

7. Each surveillance mission carried out by the Recipient shall be: (a) governed by detailed protocols prepared in accordancewith terms of reference satisfactory to the Association, requiring that such missions be: (i) under the operational command orauthority of a civilian fisheries officer; and (ii) conducted during a specific time period that is duly recorded and documented;and(b) conducted by personnel who have been properly trained in the operation of any equipment used in the surveillancemission. (Schedule 2, Section I.E, paragraph 3)

8. Upon the Association's request, the Recipient shall employ an independent expert or an independent panel of experts, as theAssociation may deem necessary, to audit periodically the surveillance activities to be carried out by the Recipient under theProject, and whose qualifications, experience and terms of reference are satisfactory to the Association. To this end, theRecipient shall take all measures required on its part, including the provision of all information required and access to allrelevant sites, to enable said expert or panel of experts, as the case may be, to conduct the audits required under, and in themanner prescribed pursuant to the provisions of the Financing Agreement. (Schedule 2, Section I.E, paragraph 4)

9. The Recipient shall: (i) take all action required to carry out the Project in accordance with the provisions and requirementsset forth or referred to in the National Project Operational Manual; (ii) submit recommendations to the Association for itsconsideration for changes and updates of the National Project Operational Manual as they may become necessary or advisable duringProject implementation in order to achieve the objectives of the Project. (Schedule 2, Section I.G)

title.narrative: 3.2. Infrastructures in priority areas transferred to the target communities management committee

comment.narrative: <p>Target not achieved. The project financed the construction and installation of 171 infrastructures in the three ZUPs, but these assets have not been legally transferred to the communities. Information source: government report “<em>Les Infrastructures Realisees dans le Cadre du Projet SWIOFish2</em>” and follow-up communication with the government.</p>

title.narrative: 2.4. Fishers in priority areas with a professional card

comment.narrative: <p>Target achieved (194%). 13,986 fishers from the three ZUPs received professional cards, whose issuance and distribution costs were covered by the project. Information source: government completion report and World Bank mission reports.</p>

title.narrative: 1.1. IOTC Compliance Support Mission (CSM) in participating countries

comment.narrative: <p>Target achieved (320%). CSM missions were carried out by the IOTC in 2019-2023 as follows: Kenya (3), Tanzania (3), Mozambique (2), Seychelles (1), Somalia (1), Comoros (2), Madagascar (2), Maldives (1), and Mauritius (1). The project paid the missions’ costs (travel, logistics, etc.). Information source: IOC completion report and World Bank mission reports.</p>

title.narrative: 3.3. Local Community Electrification Plans adopted for target communities

comment.narrative: <p>Target achieved (100%). The result reflects the adoption of 20 electrification plans for communities in Analanjirofo region (four villages), Diana region (11 villages), and Melaky region (5 villages). The electrification plans analyzed needs, installation and management costs, and sun hours, among others. The project financed the development of these plans. Information source: review of plans, government completion report, and World Bank mission reports.</p>

title.narrative: 3.1. Fishers participating in alternative fishing practices and livelihoods activities in the priority areas

comment.narrative: <p>Target partially achieved (84%). The fishers participated in alternative (non-destructive) fishing practices and fish value addition training provided by the local administration, and 769 of them, including 555 female trainees, received equipment to support these activities, such as fishery product valorization kits (sealers, vacuum bags, grinders, and pelletizers) and non-destructive fishing equipment. The fishers came from the three ZUPs. To achieve this result, the project financed value addition and market studies for each ZUP, training and awareness raising costs, and equipment costs. Information source: government completion report and World Bank mission reports.</p>

<p>Target achieved (100%). According to the World Bank, implementation was to focus on key ZUP plans’ actions, namely creation of co-managed LMMAs, local vessel and fisher registration, and stock enhancement activities, as relevant. On LMMA creation and co-management, 976.76 hectares of LMMAs were established across 18 villages with defined conservation and fishing areas, and their establishment was endorsed by the government. The villages’ fisher associations signed agreements with the respective local NGO on the joint management of the LMMAs. Vessel and fisher registration programs were carried out, as was a program that issued and distrbuted fisher professional cards to fishers (see more below). Stock enhancement activities were carried out across two of the ZUPs (in Diana and Melaky regions) and four additional regions (Antisaranana, Atsimo-Andrefanana, Boeny, and Menabe), namely restoration of 2,000 hectares of mangroves, transplanting of 4,000 m2 of coral reef, and installation of 12,000 submerged artificial habitats. The project supported these results by financing the contracts with three partner NGOs, a study on the administrative procedures governing access to fisheries resources, training and mobilization expenses for the community associations, issuance and distribution costs of the professional cards, registration radio and TV announcements, and the stock enhancement inputs. Information source: government completion report and discussions with the World Bank team.</p>

title.narrative: 3. Additional villages in priority areas accessing electricity for postharvest and value-addition activities

comment.narrative: <p>Target achieved (190%). Project-funded fish centers, ice rooms, and cold rooms/units, which are used for fish postharvest and value-addition activities, were installed with solar-powered electricity units (solar panels, batteries, and inverters) across 38 villages in the ZUPs: Ambalahonko, Ambalamanga, Ambatoloaka, Ambatozavavy, Ambodibonara, Ambodipaka, Ampapamena, Ampasimandroro, Ampasivelona, Analatsakoa (Lavanono), Andranonabo, Aniribe, Anjiamanoro, Anoromby, Antafianambitry, Antanambao Mandrisy, Antanambe, Antoraka, Antsatrana, Djangoa, Fahambahy, Fenoarivo, Fontsimaro, Hoalampano, Imorona, Mahasoa, Maintimbato, Manambolosy, Mangirankirana, Masindrano, Mozambiky, Navetsy, Nosimbola, Rantabe, Rantohely, Soahany Andriaky, Tampolo, and Tanjona. The project financed the equipment and installation costs. Information source: government report titled “<em>Les Infrastructures Realisees dans le Cadre du Projet SWIOFish2</em>”. </p>

title.narrative: 2.1. Legal texts (by-laws) for implementation of the 2015 Fisheries Law adopted by the Ministry in charge of fisheries

comment.narrative: <p>Target partially achieved (52%). The legal texts include revisions to the Fisheries Law, seven decrees, and 39 implementing texts on various issues, including aquaculture, organization of marine and continental fisheries activities, lobster fishing, commercialization and valorization of fisheries and aquaculture products, MCS, health safety of fisheries and aquaculture products and prevention of diseases, collection and export of fisheries and aquaculture products, and more. They were adopted by MPEB. To achieve this result, the project financed consultancies and legal assistance, national stakeholder validation and communication workshops, and regional awareness campaigns. Information source: government completion report and World Bank mission reports.  </p>

title.narrative: 2.2. Regions collecting and transmitting statistical catch and effort data electronically at national level to the MRHP

comment.narrative: <p>Target achieved (100%). The five regions that collected and electronically transmitted the data to MPEB’s (formerly MRHP) Directorate of Studies, Statistics and Planning were Analanjirofo, Atsimo-Andrefana, Diana, Melaky, and Menabe. The system used was FAO’s OPEN ARTFISH software application combined with a dedicated application on smartphones. To achieve this result, the project financed the application’s fees, smartphones, data collection kits and materials, recruitment and training of investigating officers on fisheries data collection measures and statistical analysis, and logistical costs. Information source: government completion report and World Bank mission reports.  </p>

title.narrative: 1.2. Annual high-level meeting of African and Indian Ocean Developing Island States (AIODIS)

comment.narrative: <p>Target partially achieved (83%). The five meetings were held in August 2018 in Seychelles, October 2019 in Mauritius, November-December 2022 in Mauritius, June 2023 in Comoros, and September 2023 in Mauritius. The project financed the meetings’ costs (travel, logistics, etc.). Information source: IOC completion, close out, and mid-term reports and World Bank mission reports.</p>

The General Assembly meetings were carried out in February 2018 in Mauritius, in October 2018 in Comoros, in October 2019 in Madagascar, in August 2021 virtually, in November 2022 in Madagascar, and in July 2023 in Réunion. The project paid for the meetings’ costs (travel, logistics, etc.). Information source: IOC completion report and World Bank mission reports.</p>

title.narrative: 2.6. Regional branch operational of the Fisheries Monitoring Center

comment.narrative: <p>Target achieved (120%). The result reflects the establishment and operationalization of FMC regional branches in Ambovombe (Androy region), Farafangana (Atsimo-Atsinanana region), Maintirano (Melaky region), Maroantsetra (Analanjirofo Region), Nosy Be (Diana region), and Toliara (Atsimo-Andrefana region). The branches had new administration offices, trained fishing inspectors, skippers, launchpads, administrative and support staff, vehicles, and monitoring plans. The project financed the construction, training, and inputs. Information source: government completion report, the government report “<em>Les Infrastructures Realisees dans le Cadre du Projet SWIOFish2</em>”, an external 2023 surveillance audit titled “<em>Rapport d'audit Final. </em><em>Auditer les activités de Surveillance réalisées par le Centre de Surveillance des Pêches (CSP) de Madagascar</em>“, and World Bank mission reports.</p>

title.narrative: 4. Share of targeted community members with rating "Satisfied" or above on project interventions (disaggregated by sex, age)

comment.narrative: <p>Target achieved (276%). The result reflects the average satisfaction rate of sampled small-scale fishers and their wives in the three ZUPs with local project interventions, including implementation of fisheries management plans, value addition training, registration, fisher card distribution, and other local activities carried out at the time of the survey. The average female satisfaction rate was 67 percent, while male satisfaction and satisfaction per age group were not analyzed. The survey was carried out by a national consulting consortium in May 2022 in the three ZUPs through individual surveys and focus group discussions in sampled fishing villages. Information source: satisfaction survey report.  </p>

title.narrative: 2.5. Small-scale fishing vessels registered and externally marked in priority areas

comment.narrative: <p>Target achieved (438%). The result reflects the number of registered and marked small-scale vessels registration and marking campaigns in the three ZUPs. The project financed registration and marking training, vessel marking design, radio and TV announcements, and marking missions’ logistics. Information source: government completion report and World Bank mission reports.</p>

title.narrative: 1. Compliance rate of SWIO countries with IOTC resolutions

comment.narrative: <p>Target not achieved. The average compliance rate of SWIO countries with IOTC resolutions was only 0.1 points above the baseline. This average result is influenced by the low results in Comoros, Mozambique, and Somalia, and at- or above-target results in Kenya, Madagascar, Maldives, Mauritius, Seychelles, South Africa, and Tanzania. The inconsistent compliance trends among the countries chalenges the attribution of the 16 project-funded compliance support missions carried out by IOTC in 2019-2023. Information source: IOTC Compliance Committee 2022 compliance reports.</p>

title.narrative: 2. Small-scale fishing units in the priority areas using prohibited gear observed during on-shore inspections

comment.narrative: <p>Target partially achieved (68%). The project achieved 68 percent of the expected reduction in the use of prohibited gear during onshore inspections in the three ZUPs. The reduction was thanks to project-financed establishment and operationalization of six FMC regional branches, in Androy, Analanjirofo, Atsimo-Andrefana, Atsimo-Atsinanana, Diana, and Melaky regions, training of deployed fisheries inspectors, maintenance of two FMC surveillance vessels, and acquisition of inspection vehicles, speedboats, and drones for the central and regional FMC offices. Information source: government completion report.</p>
